title: Constructions — Complete Learning Module (Learn Maths with Fun)
outcomes: Divide a line segment internally in a given ratio using a ruler and compass
Construct a triangle similar to a given triangle with a given scale factor (both smaller and larger)
Construct tangents to a circle from an external point using geometric methods
Construct a triangle with specific constraints using ruler and compass
Understand why each construction works through geometric reasoning
Apply construction techniques in real-world Indian contexts like land surveying and architecture
Solve RD Sharma and RS Aggarwal extension problems for competitive exam readiness

concepts.name: Division of a Line Segment in a Given Ratio
concepts.real_life_application: When dividing a plot of land among siblings in a ratio of 2:3 at a village panchayat in Uttar Pradesh, you need to mark the exact division point on the boundary line.
concepts.purpose: Learn to divide any line segment into any ratio precisely without measuring — a fundamental skill in surveying, architecture, and map-making.
day_to_day_usage: Dividing inherited agricultural land among family members in specific ratios
Marking boundary walls during construction of a housing colony in Pune
Laying out running tracks of proportional lengths in a school playground
Setting up tent pegs in a marriage pandal at specified distances
Architects marking window placements along a wall in a given proportion

concepts.industry_relevance: Math is the engine of AI, finance, engineering and space — this concept is used daily by data scientists and engineers.

concepts.name: Construction of Tangents to a Circle
concepts.real_life_application: A gardener at Lodhi Garden, Delhi, is laying a circular flower bed. She needs to place sprinklers that spray water tangentially to the circle to cover the surrounding grass area without wasting water inside the bed.
concepts.purpose: Tangents appear everywhere: the wheels of a train on tracks (wheel touches rail at a tangent), the string of a kite at its highest point, and the line of sight from a point outside a circular park.
day_to_day_usage: A train wheel touching the railway track at exactly one point (tangent)
The direction of water spray from a rotating sprinkler at a 45° angle
A satellite dish oriented at a tangent angle to receive optimal signal
A car taking a sharp turn on a circular road — the direction of motion is tangential

theorems.name: Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales Theorem) — Applied in Constructions
theorems.statement: If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle intersecting the other two sides, it divides those sides in the same ratio.

proposed_by.name: Thales of Miletus
proposed_by.known_as: First known philosopher and mathematician in Western tradition

theorems.historical_context: Thales is credited with being the first to use deductive reasoning in geometry. He measured the height of the Egyptian pyramids by comparing shadows — the same proportional reasoning that underlies the BPT. This theorem is used to justify why our construction method for dividing a line segment works.
theorems.why_proposed: Thales needed a theoretical foundation for measuring inaccessible heights and distances. His theorem showed that proportional relationships hold in any triangle when a parallel line is drawn — a principle used in surveying for millennia.
theorems.real_world_utility: Used in: (1) Map scaling and surveying; (2) Divide any length in a given ratio; (3) Determining heights of buildings using shadow measurement; (4) Navigation and triangulation systems.
theorems.why_students_learn: This theorem is the basis for the line segment division construction. Understanding WHY the construction works is more important than just memorizing steps — it teaches deductive reasoning.

examples.problem: A 12m long wall needs to be divided in the ratio 3:2 to allocate space for two shops in a market complex. Using the concept of parallel lines, determine where the partition should be placed.
examples.indiandiaspora_context: A shopkeeper in Chandni Chowk, Delhi, is renovating his shop and needs to divide the wall space between two product sections.
solution_step_by_step: Step 2: Length of first section = (3/5) × 12 = 7.2 m
Step 3: Length of second section = (2/5) × 12 = 4.8 m
Step 4: The partition should be placed 7.2 m from one end.
Step 5: To construct this on paper: draw a ray at an acute angle from one end, mark 5 equal arcs of any convenient length, join the 5th mark to the other end, and draw parallels through the 3rd mark.
examples.final_answer: The partition wall is placed 7.2 m from one end, creating sections of 7.2 m and 4.8 m.

theorems.name: Tangent-Radius Theorem
theorems.statement: The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
theorems.historical_context: Euclid's Book III of Elements deals entirely with circles. Proposition 18 states this theorem. It is the foundation for constructing tangents to circles — we use this property (90° angle) to locate the point of tangency.
theorems.why_proposed: Understanding the tangent-radius relationship is essential for constructing tangents. The fact that OP ⟂ tangent at P means that if we can locate the point P such that OP makes 90° with the tangent, we can draw the tangent.
theorems.real_world_utility: (1) Designing circular roads with tangential exits; (2) Gear systems in automobiles where teeth make tangential contact; (3) Optical instruments where light rays hit lenses tangentially; (4) Roundabout traffic circles with tangential entry/exit roads.
theorems.why_students_learn: This theorem is the key to constructing tangents from an external point. The construction relies on creating a right angle at the point of tangency using the diameter property (angle in a semicircle is 90°).

examples.problem: A circular park of radius 50 m has a lamp post 130 m away from the center. What is the length of the tangent (straight-line walking path) from the lamp post to the point where it touches the park boundary?
solution_step_by_step: Step 1: Let O be the center, P be the lamp post. OP = 130 m.
Step 2: Let T be the point where the path touches the park (tangency point).
Step 3: By the theorem, OT ⟂ PT. So triangle OTP is right-angled at T.
Step 5: Using Pythagoras: PT² = OP² - OT² = 130² - 50² = 16900 - 2500 = 14400
Step 7: The walking path from the lamp post to the park is 120 m.
examples.final_answer: Length of the tangent path = 120 m.

important_formulae.name: Scale Factor for Similar Triangles
important_formulae.formula: If scale factor = k (k > 1 for larger, k < 1 for smaller), then each side of the new triangle = k × corresponding side of original triangle.
important_formulae.explanation: When constructing a triangle similar to a given triangle, we use a scale factor. Example: Construct ΔABC ∼ ΔPQR with scale factor 3/4 means each side of ABC is 3/4 of the corresponding side of PQR (ABC is smaller).
important_formulae.usage: Scale factor > 1 → Enlargement; Scale factor < 1 → Reduction

important_formulae.name: Number of Tangents from a Point
important_formulae.formula: From a point inside a circle: 0 tangents; On the circle: 1 tangent; Outside the circle: 2 tangents.
important_formulae.explanation: The number of tangents depends on the position of the point relative to the circle. This determines which construction method to use.
important_formulae.usage: Only external point construction is covered in NCERT Class 10.

important_formulae.name: Length of Tangent
important_formulae.formula: Length of tangent from external point P to point of contact T: PT = √(OP² - r²), where O is the center and r is the radius.
important_formulae.explanation: Derived from the Tangent-Radius theorem using Pythagoras.
important_formulae.usage: This formula is frequently used in both board and competitive exams.

worked_examples.problem: Draw a line segment AB of length 8 cm. Divide it internally in the ratio 3:4. Write the steps of construction.
board_mode: Step 1: Draw a ray AX making an acute angle with AB.
Step 2: On AX, mark 7 (3+4) equal arcs: A₁, A₂, A₃, A₄, A₅, A₆, A₇ such that AA₁ = A₁A₂ = A₂A₃ = A₃A₄ = A₄A₅ = A₅A₆ = A₆A₇.
Step 3: Join A₇ to B.
Step 4: Draw a line through A₃ parallel to A₇B (by constructing ∠AA₃P = ∠AA₇B) meeting AB at P.
Step 5: P divides AB in the ratio 3:4, i.e., AP:PB = 3:4.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: Ensure arcs on AX are EQUAL. Use a compass to mark them. The number of arcs = sum of ratio terms (3+4=7). The division point corresponds to the first term (3rd arc).
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: For JEE, know the logic: By BPT, if lines through A₃ and A₇ are parallel, then AA₃/A₃A₇ = AP/PB = 3/4. The construction directly applies Thales theorem.

worked_examples.problem: Construct a triangle similar to ΔABC with sides 5 cm, 6 cm, and 7 cm, with scale factor 3/5. Write construction steps and verify.
board_mode: Step 1: Construct ΔABC with AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 7 cm.
Step 2: Draw a ray BX making an acute angle with BC on the side opposite to A.
Step 3: Mark 5 equal arcs on BX: B₁, B₂, B₃, B₄, B₅ (since scale denominator is 5).
Step 4: Join B₅ to C.
Step 5: Draw a line through B₃ (3rd point, since numerator = 3) parallel to B₅C to meet BC at C'.
Step 6: Draw a line through C' parallel to CA to meet BA at A'.
Step 7: ΔA'BC' is the required triangle with scale factor 3/5.
Verification: BC' = (3/5) × BC = (3/5) × 6 = 3.6 cm
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: If scale factor = m/n, mark n arcs on the ray. Draw line from nth arc to the opposite vertex. Draw parallel through mth arc. If m < n, triangle is smaller; if m > n, triangle is larger.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: The construction uses BPT in reverse. B₃C' ∥ B₅C implies that BC'/BC = BB₃/BB₅ = 3/5.

worked_examples.topic: Construction of Tangents to a Circle from an External Point
worked_examples.problem: Draw a circle of radius 4 cm. Take a point P at a distance of 7 cm from the center. Construct two tangents from P to the circle. Measure their lengths.
board_mode: Step 1: Draw a circle with center O and radius 4 cm.
Step 2: Mark point P such that OP = 7 cm.
Step 3: Find the midpoint M of OP by drawing the perpendicular bisector.
Step 4: Draw a circle with center M and radius MO = MP.
Step 5: This circle intersects the original circle at points T₁ and T₂.
Step 6: Join PT₁ and PT₂. These are the required tangents.
Step 7: Measure PT₁ and PT₂. By Pythagoras: PT = √(7² - 4²) = √(49-16) = √33 ≈ 5.74 cm.
Note: T₁ and T₂ are the points of tangency. The construction works because ∠OT₁P = 90° (angle in a semicircle), and by Tangent-Radius theorem, OT₁ ⟂ PT₁.
worked_examples.speed_mode: Golden step: The key is constructing the midpoint of OP and drawing the circle with OP as diameter. The intersection points give exactly the right tangency points because the angle in a semicircle is 90°.
worked_examples.competitive_shortcut: Length of tangent can be found directly: PT = √(OP² - r²) = √(49 - 16) = √33 ≈ 5.74 cm. The construction is essentially creating a right-angled triangle OTP where angle T = 90°.

exercise_1.title: Exercise — Division of a Line Segment and Similar Triangles
exercise_1.objective: Practice constructing line divisions and similar triangles with given scale factors

problems.question: Draw a line segment of length 7.6 cm and divide it in the ratio 5:8. Measure the two parts.
solution: Step 1: Draw AB = 7.6 cm.
Step 2: Draw ray AX making an acute angle with AB.
Step 3: Mark 13 equal arcs (5+8) on AX: A₁, A₂, ..., A₁₃.
Step 4: Join A₁₃ to B.
Step 5: Through A₅, draw a line parallel to A₁₃B meeting AB at P.
Step 6: AP:PB = 5:8.
problems.concept_insight: The number of arcs must equal the sum of the ratio terms (5+8=13). The parallel through the 5th arc ensures BPT gives the 5:8 ratio.

problems.question: Draw a line segment of length 7.6 cm and divide it internally in the ratio 5:7. Also give the justification of the construction.
solution: Construction:
Step 1: Draw AB = 7.6 cm.
Step 2: Draw ray AX making acute angle with AB.
Step 3: On AX, mark 12 equal arcs: A₁, A₂, ..., A₁₂.
Step 4: Join A₁₂B.
Step 5: Through A₅, draw A₅P ∥ A₁₂B (by making ∠AA₅P = ∠AA₁₂B) meeting AB at P.
Step 6: P divides AB in ratio 5:7, i.e., AP:PB = 5:7.
Justification:
In ΔAA₁₂B, we have drawn A₅P ∥ A₁₂B.
By BPT (Thales Theorem): AA₅/A₅A₁₂ = AP/PB.
Since AA₅ = 5 equal arcs and A₅A₁₂ = 7 equal arcs: AA₅/A₅A₁₂ = 5/7.
Therefore, AP/PB = 5/7. Hence, AP:PB = 5:7.
problems.final_answer: P divides AB such that AP:PB = 5:7.
problems.concept_insight: Justification is important for board exams. Always cite Basic Proportionality Theorem to explain why the construction works.

problems.question: Draw a line segment AB of length 8 cm. Taking A as center, draw a circle of radius 4 cm and taking B as center, draw another circle of radius 3 cm. Construct tangents to each circle from the center of the other circle.
solution: Step 1: Draw AB = 8 cm.
Step 2: Draw circle with center A, radius 4 cm.
Step 3: Draw circle with center B, radius 3 cm.
Tangents from B to circle centered at A:
Step 4: Find midpoint M₁ of AB.
Step 5: Draw circle with center M₁, radius M₁A = M₁B, intersecting circle A at T₁ and T₂.
Step 6: Join BT₁ and BT₂. These are tangents from B to circle A.
Tangents from A to circle centered at B:
Step 7: Find midpoint M₂ of AB (same as M₁).
Step 8: The same circle with center M₁ intersects circle B at T₃ and T₄.
Step 9: Join AT₃ and AT₄. These are tangents from A to circle B.
Verification: AT₁ = radius of circle A = 4 cm, but BT₁ = √(8² - 4²) = √48 ≈ 6.93 cm.
Similarly, BT₃ = radius of circle B = 3 cm, AT₃ = √(8² - 3²) = √55 ≈ 7.42 cm.
problems.final_answer: Tangents constructed from each center to the other circle.
problems.concept_insight: The same semicircle construction works because OP becomes the diameter of the new circle, ensuring right angle at the point of tangency.

problems.question: Draw two concentric circles of radii 3 cm and 5 cm. Take a point on the outer circle and construct the pair of tangents to the inner circle.
solution: Step 1: Draw concentric circles with center O: inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 5 cm.
Step 2: Take any point P on the outer circle. OP = 5 cm.
Step 3: Find midpoint M of OP.
Step 4: Draw circle with center M, radius MO = MP.
Step 5: This circle intersects the inner circle at T₁ and T₂.
Step 6: Join PT₁ and PT₂. These are tangents from P to the inner circle.
Verification: Length PT₁ = PT₂ = √(OP² - r²) = √(25 - 9) = √16 = 4 cm.
problems.final_answer: Tangents PT₁ and PT₂ constructed. Length of each tangent = 4 cm.
problems.concept_insight: Even though P is on a circle, we're drawing tangents to a DIFFERENT (inner) circle from P. P is external to the inner circle.

problems.question: Draw a triangle ABC with side BC = 6 cm, AB = 5 cm, and ∠ABC = 60°. Then construct a triangle whose sides are 3/4 of the corresponding sides of ΔABC.
solution: Step 1: Construct ΔABC: draw BC = 6 cm. At B, construct ∠XBC = 60°. With B as center, radius 5 cm, cut BX at A. Join AC.
Step 2: Draw ray BY making acute angle with BC on the side opposite to A.
Step 3: Mark 4 equal arcs on BY: B₁, B₂, B₃, B₄.
Step 4: Join B₄ to C.
Step 5: Through B₃ (since numerator = 3), draw B₃C' ∥ B₄C, meeting BC at C'.
Step 6: Through C', draw C'A' ∥ CA, meeting BA at A'.
Step 7: ΔA'BC' is the required triangle with scale factor 3/4.
Verification: BC' = (3/4) × 6 = 4.5 cm, A'B = (3/4) × 5 = 3.75 cm.
In ΔABC, by cosine rule: AC² = AB² + BC² - 2(AB)(BC)cos60° = 25 + 36 - 60(0.5) = 31.
problems.final_answer: Triangle A'BC' is the required triangle with scale factor 3/4.
problems.concept_insight: Scale factor 3/4 < 1, so the new triangle is smaller. Always mark number of arcs = denominator of scale factor (4), and draw parallel through numerator (3rd arc).

problems.question: Draw a triangle ABC with side BC = 7 cm, ∠B = 45°, ∠A = 105°. Then construct a triangle whose sides are 4/3 times the corresponding sides of ΔABC.
solution: Step 1: Construct ΔABC: draw BC = 7 cm. At B, construct ∠B = 45°. At A, we have ∠A = 105°, so ∠C = 180° - (45° + 105°) = 30°.
Step 2: At C, construct ∠C = 30°. Rays from B (45°) and C (30°) intersect at A.
Step 3: Draw ray BX making acute angle with BC on the side opposite to A.
Step 4: Mark 3 equal arcs on BX: B₁, B₂, B₃ (since denominator = 3).
Step 5: Join B₃ to C.
Step 6: Since scale factor 4/3 > 1, we extend BC beyond C. Through B₄ (4th arc, extend BX to B₄), draw B₄C' ∥ B₃C extending BC beyond C to meet at C'.
Step 7: Through C', draw C'A' ∥ CA extending BA beyond A to meet at A'.
Step 8: ΔA'BC' is the required triangle with scale factor 4/3.
Verification: BC' = (4/3) × BC = (4/3) × 7 = 9.33 cm.
The new triangle is larger since scale factor > 1.
problems.final_answer: Triangle A'BC' is the required triangle with scale factor 4/3.
problems.concept_insight: For scale factor > 1 (enlargement), extend BC beyond C and use arcs beyond the denominator count. The construction is essentially the same but on the extended side.

problems.question: Draw a right triangle in which the sides (other than hypotenuse) are of lengths 4 cm and 3 cm. Then construct another triangle whose sides are 5/3 times the corresponding sides of the given triangle.
solution: Step 1: Construct right ΔABC with ∠B = 90°, AB = 4 cm, BC = 3 cm.
Step 2: By Pythagoras: AC = √(4² + 3²) = 5 cm (3-4-5 triangle).
Step 3: Draw ray BX making acute angle with BC on the side opposite to A.
Step 4: Mark 3 equal arcs on BX: B₁, B₂, B₃.
Step 5: Join B₃ to C.
Step 6: Extend BX to B₅. Through B₅, draw B₅C' ∥ B₃C extending BC beyond C to meet at C'.
Step 7: Through C', draw C'A' ∥ CA extending BA beyond A to meet at A'.
Step 8: ΔA'BC' is required. Scale factor 5/3:
problems.final_answer: Triangle A'BC' constructed with sides 5/3 times ΔABC.
problems.concept_insight: The 3-4-5 right triangle is a Pythagorean triple. Scale factor 5/3 gives sides 5 cm, 6.67 cm, 8.33 cm — check: 6.67² + 5² ≈ 44.49 + 25 = 69.49 ≈ 8.33² = 69.39 ✓

exercise_2.title: Exercise — Construction of Tangents to a Circle
exercise_2.objective: Construct tangents from external points and justify constructions

problems.question: Draw a circle of radius 6 cm. From a point 10 cm away from its center, construct the pair of tangents to the circle and measure their lengths.
solution: Step 1: Draw circle with center O, radius 6 cm.
Step 2: Mark point P such that OP = 10 cm.
Step 3: Find midpoint M of OP.
Step 4: Draw circle with center M, radius MO = MP = 5 cm.
Step 5: Mark intersection points of the two circles as T₁ and T₂.
Step 6: Join PT₁ and PT₂.
Step 7: By Tangent-Radius theorem, OT₁ ⟂ PT₁ and OT₂ ⟂ PT₂.
Step 8: Length PT = √(OP² - r²) = √(100 - 36) = √64 = 8 cm.
Step 9: Measure PT₁ and PT₂ — both should be 8 cm.
problems.final_answer: Tangents constructed. Length of each tangent = 8 cm.
problems.concept_insight: Always verify with the formula PT = √(OP² - r²). The construction works because ∠OT₁P is 90° (angle in a semicircle with OP as diameter).

problems.question: Draw a circle of radius 4 cm. Take a point P on its circumference. Construct the tangent to the circle at P. Give justification.
solution: Construction:
Step 1: Draw circle with center O, radius 4 cm. Mark point P on the circle.
Step 2: Join OP.
Step 3: At P, construct a line perpendicular to OP using a protractor or by drawing a 90° angle.
Step 4: This line is the required tangent at P.
Justification:
By the Tangent-Radius theorem, the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.
Since we constructed PT ⟂ OP, PT is the tangent at P.
problems.final_answer: Tangent constructed at point P on the circle.
problems.concept_insight: For a point ON the circle, we construct the perpendicular to the radius. For a point OUTSIDE the circle, we use the semicircle method.

problems.question: Draw a circle of radius 3 cm. Take two points P and Q on one of its extended diameters on opposite sides of the circle, each at a distance of 7 cm from the center. Draw tangents to the circle from these two points P and Q.
solution: Step 1: Draw circle with center O, radius 3 cm.
Step 2: Draw a diameter AB. Extend it on both sides.
Step 3: Mark P on the left extension and Q on the right extension such that OP = OQ = 7 cm.
Tangents from P:
Step 4: Find midpoint M₁ of OP.
Step 5: Draw circle with center M₁, radius M₁O, intersecting original circle at T₁ and T₂.
Step 6: Join PT₁ and PT₂. These are tangents from P.
Tangents from Q:
Step 7: Find midpoint M₂ of OQ.
Step 8: Draw circle with center M₂, radius M₂O, intersecting original circle at T₃ and T₄.
Step 9: Join QT₃ and QT₄. These are tangents from Q.
Length of each tangent = √(49 - 9) = √40 = 2√10 ≈ 6.32 cm.
problems.final_answer: Two tangents from P and two tangents from Q constructed. Each tangent length ≈ 6.32 cm.
problems.concept_insight: Points P and Q are symmetric about O. The tangents from P and Q have equal lengths since both are at the same distance from the center.

problems.question: Draw a pair of tangents to a circle of radius 5 cm which are inclined to each other at an angle of 60°. Write the steps of construction.
solution: Step 1: Draw circle with center O, radius 5 cm.
Step 2: Draw radius OA.
Step 3: At O, construct an angle of 120° (since 180° - 60° = 120°) with OA to get ray OB.
Step 4: Draw tangents at A and B (perpendicular to OA and OB respectively).
Step 5: Let these tangents intersect at point P.
Step 6: PA and PB are the required tangents inclined at 60°.
Justification: In quadrilateral OAPB, ∠A = ∠B = 90° (radius ⟂ tangent).
∠AOB = 120° (by construction).
Sum of angles = 90° + 90° + 120° + ∠APB = 360°
So ∠APB = 60°. Hence the tangents are inclined at 60°.
Length of each tangent: In right ΔOAP, OP = OA/sin(60°) = 5/(√3/2) = 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 cm.
problems.final_answer: Tangents PA and PB constructed inclined at 60°.
problems.concept_insight: Angle between tangents + angle between radii = 180°. So if ∠APB = 60°, then ∠AOB = 120°. This is a key result: the quadrilateral formed by radii and tangents is cyclic with sum of opposite angles = 180°.

problems.question: Draw a circle of radius 4 cm with center O. Take a point P outside the circle such that OP = 8 cm. Construct tangents from P to the circle. Verify by measuring the angle between the tangents.
solution: Step 1: Draw circle with center O, radius 4 cm.
Step 2: Mark P such that OP = 8 cm.
Step 3: Find midpoint M of OP.
Step 4: Draw circle with center M, radius MO = MP = 4 cm.
Step 5: Mark intersections T₁ and T₂ of the two circles.
Step 6: Join PT₁ and PT₂.
Verification of angle:
In right ΔOT₁P: sin(∠OPT₁) = OT₁/OP = 4/8 = 1/2, so ∠OPT₁ = 30°.
By symmetry, ∠OPT₂ = 30°.
So ∠T₁PT₂ = 60°.
Length of tangent PT₁ = √(64 - 16) = √48 = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm.
problems.final_answer: Tangents constructed. Angle between tangents = 60°. Length of each tangent = 4√3 ≈ 6.93 cm.
problems.concept_insight: When OP = 2r, the angle between tangents is 60° (since sin(θ/2) = r/OP = 1/2 → θ/2 = 30° → θ = 60°).

topics.name: Construction of a Triangle Similar to a Given Triangle with Scale Factor m:n
topics.concept: When the scale factor m:n involves a ratio not in simplest form, or when the triangle to be constructed is to be positioned differently, additional steps may be needed.

examples.problem: Construct a triangle similar to ΔPQR with sides PQ = 6 cm, QR = 7 cm, PR = 8 cm, with scale factor 5:3. Write all construction steps.
solution: Step 1: Construct ΔPQR with given sides.
Step 2: Draw ray QX making an acute angle with QR on the side opposite to P.
Step 3: Mark 3 equal arcs on QX (since denominator = 3): Q₁, Q₂, Q₃.
Step 4: Since scale factor 5/3 > 1, extend QR beyond R.
Step 5: Extend QX beyond Q₃. Join Q₃ to R.
Step 6: On extended QX, mark Q₄ and Q₅ beyond Q₃.
Step 7: Through Q₅, draw Q₅R' ∥ Q₃R meeting extended QR at R'.
Step 8: Through R', draw R'P' ∥ RP meeting extended QP at P'.
Step 9: ΔP'QR' is the required triangle with sides 5/3 times ΔPQR.

topics.competitive_note: In competitive exams, the scale factor may be given as a rational number like 2.5 (which is 5/2). Convert to improper fraction first. Also, questions may ask to construct without showing the base triangle first.

topics.name: Construction When One Side and Angles Are Given
topics.concept: Given a triangle with specific dimensions and a scale factor, construct the similar triangle.

examples.problem: Construct ΔABC with BC = 8 cm, ∠B = 45°, ∠C = 60°. Then construct ΔA'BC' similar to ΔABC with scale factor 3/2.
solution: Step 1: Construct ΔABC: BC = 8 cm, ∠B = 45°, ∠C = 60°.
Step 2: By angle sum: ∠A = 180° - 45° - 60° = 75°.
Step 3: Draw ray BX making acute angle with BC.
Step 4: Mark 2 equal arcs: B₁, B₂.
Step 5: Extend BX to B₃. Through B₃, draw B₃C' ∥ B₂C extending BC beyond C to C'.
Step 6: Through C', draw C'A' ∥ CA extending BA beyond A to A'.
Step 7: ΔA'BC' is the required triangle.

topics.name: Construction of Tangents Without Using Center
topics.concept: When the center of the circle is not known, we can still construct a tangent at a given point using a different method involving chords.
topics.method: Draw a chord through the given point, construct its perpendicular bisector, and use the property of angles in alternate segments.

examples.problem: Given a circle without a marked center, draw a tangent at a point P on the circle.
solution: Step 1: Mark point P on the circle.
Step 2: Draw any chord PQ through P.
Step 3: At Q, draw a line QR such that ∠PQR = ∠R (construct angle equal to the angle in the alternate segment).
Alternative method:
Step 1: Draw chord PA.
Step 2: Construct ∠PAB = ∠APB on the opposite side of chord PA.
Step 3: Extend AB. This is the tangent at P.
examples.final_answer: Tangent constructed at P without using the center.

topics.competitive_note: This method uses the alternate segment theorem: the angle between a tangent and a chord through the point of contact equals the angle in the alternate segment.

topics.name: Construction of Incircle and Circumcircle
topics.concept: The incircle touches all three sides of a triangle (center = intersection of angle bisectors). The circumcircle passes through all three vertices (center = intersection of perpendicular bisectors).

examples.problem: Construct ΔABC with sides AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, CA = 7 cm. Construct its incircle. Measure the inradius.
solution: Step 1: Construct ΔABC with given sides.
Step 2: Draw angle bisectors of ∠A and ∠B. Their intersection is I, the incenter.
Step 3: From I, draw perpendicular to any side (e.g., BC) meeting at D.
Step 4: Draw circle with center I and radius ID.
Step 5: This circle touches all three sides — this is the incircle.
To compute inradius: using area = rs, where s = (5+6+7)/2 = 9.
Inradius r = Area/s = 14.70/9 ≈ 1.63 cm.

simple.question: Draw a line segment AB of length 10 cm. Divide it internally in the ratio 3:4. Write the steps of construction and measure the two parts.
simple.answer: The segment is divided at point P such that AP:PB = 3:4. AP ≈ 4.29 cm, PB ≈ 5.71 cm.
steps: Draw AB = 10 cm.
Draw ray AX making an acute angle with AB.
On AX, mark 7 equal arcs (3+4): A₁, A₂, ..., A₇ such that AA₁ = A₁A₂ = ... = A₆A₇.
Join A₇ to B.
Draw a line through A₃ parallel to A₇B meeting AB at P.
hints: Number of arcs = sum of ratio terms.
The parallel line uses Basic Proportionality Theorem.

simple.question: Draw a circle of radius 3 cm. Take a point P at a distance of 7 cm from its center. Construct a pair of tangents from P to the circle. Measure the length of one tangent.
steps: Draw circle with center O and radius 3 cm.
Mark point P such that OP = 7 cm.
Find the midpoint M of OP by drawing perpendicular bisector.
Draw a circle with center M and radius MO = MP.
Mark intersection points T₁ and T₂ of the two circles.
Join PT₁ and PT₂. These are the required tangents.
hints: The angle in a semicircle is 90°, giving the right angle needed.
Use the formula PT = √(OP² - r²) to verify the length.

medium.question: Draw a triangle ABC with BC = 6 cm, AB = 5 cm, and ∠ABC = 60°. Then construct a triangle whose sides are 4/3 times the corresponding sides of ΔABC. Justify the construction.
medium.answer: ΔA'BC' is the required triangle with scale factor 4/3. BC' = 8 cm, A'B = 6.67 cm.
steps: Construct ΔABC: draw BC = 6 cm, at B make 60°, cut BA = 5 cm, join AC.
Draw ray BX making acute angle with BC on side opposite to A.
Mark 3 equal arcs on BX: B₁, B₂, B₃.
Extend BX to B₄ (since numerator 4 > denominator 3).
Join B₃ to C.
Through B₄, draw B₄C' ∥ B₃C extending BC beyond C to meet at C'.
Through C', draw C'A' ∥ CA extending BA beyond A to meet at A'.
ΔA'BC' is the required triangle. Justification: By BPT, BC'/BC = BB₄/BB₃ = 4/3.
hints: Scale factor > 1 means the new triangle is larger — extend the sides.
Number of arcs on ray = denominator (3); parallel through numerator (4th arc).

medium.question: Draw a pair of tangents to a circle of radius 4 cm which are inclined to each other at an angle of 75°. Write the steps of construction.
medium.answer: Tangents PA and PB constructed with ∠APB = 75°. Length of each tangent ≈ 3.06 cm.
steps: Draw circle with center O and radius 4 cm.
Draw radius OA.
At O, construct an angle of 105° (since 180° - 75° = 105°) with OA to get ray OB.
Draw tangents at A and B perpendicular to OA and OB respectively.
Let the tangents intersect at point P.
PA and PB are the required tangents inclined at 75°.
Justification: ∠OAP = ∠OBP = 90°, ∠AOB = 105°, so ∠APB = 360° - 90° - 90° - 105° = 75°.
hints: Angle between tangents + angle between radii = 180°.
Use the property of quadrilateral OAPB.

complex.question: Draw a circle of radius 5 cm. Take two points P and Q at distances 8 cm and 12 cm respectively from the center, on the same side of the center. Construct tangents from both points to the circle. Without measuring by scale, determine mathematically which set of tangents is longer and by how much.
complex.answer: From P: PT = √(64 - 25) = √39 ≈ 6.24 cm. From Q: QT = √(144 - 25) = √119 ≈ 10.91 cm. Tangents from Q are longer by √119 - √39 ≈ 4.67 cm.
steps: Draw circle with center O and radius 5 cm.
Mark P on the same side such that OP = 8 cm.
Mark Q further out such that OQ = 12 cm.
Construct tangents from P: find midpoint M₁ of OP, draw circle(M₁, M₁O) intersecting original circle at T₁, T₂. Join PT₁, PT₂.
Construct tangents from Q: find midpoint M₂ of OQ, draw circle(M₂, M₂O) intersecting original circle at T₃, T₄. Join QT₃, QT₄.
Length PT = √(OP² - r²) = √(64 - 25) = √39 cm.
Length QT = √(OQ² - r²) = √(144 - 25) = √119 cm.
Since √119 > √39, tangents from Q are longer by √119 - √39 cm ≈ 4.67 cm.
hints: The length formula PT = √(OP² - r²) depends only on OP, not direction.
Compare squares: OP² - r² vs OQ² - r² — the farther point gives longer tangents.

complex.question: Construct a right triangle with legs 6 cm and 8 cm. Construct a triangle similar to it with scale factor 2/3. Verify using Pythagoras theorem that the new triangle is also right-angled.
complex.answer: New triangle sides: 4 cm, 5.33 cm, 6.67 cm. Check: 4² + 5.33² = 16 + 28.44 = 44.44 ≈ 6.67² ✓
steps: Construct right ΔABC with ∠B = 90°, AB = 6 cm, BC = 8 cm. AC = √(36 + 64) = 10 cm.
Draw ray BX making acute angle with BC on side opposite to A.
Mark 3 equal arcs: B₁, B₂, B₃.
Join B₃ to C.
Through B₂ (since numerator = 2), draw B₂C' ∥ B₃C meeting BC at C'.
Through C', draw C'A' ∥ CA meeting BA at A'.
ΔA'BC' is the required triangle. Sides: A'B = (2/3) × 6 = 4 cm, BC' = (2/3) × 8 = 16/3 ≈ 5.33 cm, A'C' = (2/3) × 10 = 20/3 ≈ 6.67 cm.
Verification: 4² + (16/3)² = 16 + 256/9 = (144 + 256)/9 = 400/9 = (20/3)². Hence right-angled at B.
hints: Scale factor 2/3 < 1, so the new triangle is smaller than the original.
Similar triangles preserve angles — a right triangle stays right-angled after similarity transformation.

simple.question: What is the minimum number of arcs to be marked on the ray to divide a line segment in the ratio 3:4?

explanation.correct: We need to mark (3+4) = 7 equal arcs on the auxiliary ray.

wrong_options.1: 3 is only one part of the ratio. Total arcs = sum of ratio terms.
wrong_options.2: 4 is only the second part. Total arcs = sum of ratio terms.
wrong_options.3: 12 is the product, not the sum. Total arcs = numerator + denominator.

simple.question: How many tangents can be drawn to a circle from a point outside the circle?

explanation.correct: Exactly 2 tangents can be drawn from an external point to a circle — one on each side.

wrong_options.1: Only 1 tangent exists for a point ON the circle, not outside.
wrong_options.2: 0 tangents from a point INSIDE the circle.
wrong_options.3: Infinite tangents don't exist — only 2 specific lines from the point satisfy the tangent condition.

simple.question: The tangent at a point on a circle is perpendicular to:
options: The radius at the point of contact
The diameter at the opposite end

explanation.correct: Tangent-Radius theorem: The tangent is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of contact.

wrong_options.1: The diameter at the opposite end is not related to the tangent at a point.
wrong_options.2: A chord and tangent are not necessarily perpendicular.
wrong_options.3: Two tangents from the same external point are equal in length but not perpendicular to each other.

simple.question: Which theorem is used in the justification of dividing a line segment in a given ratio?

explanation.correct: BPT (Thales Theorem) states that if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle, it divides the other two sides proportionally.

wrong_options.1: Pythagoras theorem deals with right triangles, not proportional division.
wrong_options.2: Tangent-Radius theorem is for circles.
wrong_options.3: Angle sum property is about triangles summing to 180°.

simple.question: The angle between the tangents drawn from an external point P to a circle is related to the angle between the radii as:

explanation.correct: In quadrilateral OAPB (where A, B are points of tangency): ∠A = ∠B = 90°, so ∠AOB + ∠APB = 180°.

wrong_options.1: 90° is not correct — the sum is 180°.
wrong_options.2: They are not equal; they are supplementary.
wrong_options.3: Product relationship doesn't exist.

simple.question: For constructing a triangle similar to a given triangle with scale factor 3/5, the new triangle will be:

explanation.correct: Scale factor = 3/5 = 0.6 < 1, so the new triangle is smaller than the original.

wrong_options.1: Larger only if scale factor > 1.
wrong_options.2: Same size only if scale factor = 1.
wrong_options.3: It can be determined: compare scale factor with 1.

simple.question: What is the length of tangent from a point at distance 5 cm from center if radius = 3 cm?

wrong_options.1: 2 cm would need OP² - r² = 4 → 25 - r² = 4 → r² = 21, not matching.
wrong_options.2: 8 cm would be OP + r, not correct.
wrong_options.3: √34 would be OP² + r², but it's OP² - r².

simple.question: In the construction of tangents, the circle drawn on OP as diameter is used because:
options: It divides the circle into two equal parts

explanation.correct: Angle in a semicircle is 90°. Since OT ⟂ PT (Tangent-Radius theorem), ∠OTP must be 90°, which is the angle in a semicircle with OP as diameter.

wrong_options.1: This is a property but not the reason for the construction.
wrong_options.2: The circle passes through many points, not relevant here.
wrong_options.3: The construction uses the 90° angle property, not equal parts.

simple.question: If OP = 2r (distance of external point is twice the radius), the angle between tangents is:

explanation.correct: If OP = 2r, then sin(θ/2) = r/OP = 1/2, so θ/2 = 30°, θ = 60°.

wrong_options.1: 30° would be half the angle, not the total.
wrong_options.2: 90° would need OP = r√2.
wrong_options.3: 45° would need sin(22.5°) = r/OP, giving OP ≈ 2.61r.

simple.question: How many arcs are marked on the auxiliary ray when constructing a triangle similar to a given triangle with scale factor 5/3?

explanation.correct: For scale factor m/n, we mark 'n' arcs (the denominator) on the auxiliary ray. Here n = 3.

wrong_options.1: 5 is the numerator, not the number of arcs. Arcs = denominator.
wrong_options.2: 8 is the sum of numerator and denominator. For similar triangles, arcs = denominator only.
wrong_options.3: 15 is the product of numerator and denominator.

medium.question: To divide a line segment AB in the ratio m:n, we draw a ray AX. On AX, we mark (m+n) equal arcs and join the last arc to B. Then through the point corresponding to which arc number do we draw the parallel line?

explanation.correct: Through the mth arc (the first part of the ratio), we draw the line parallel to the line joining the last arc to B. This gives AP:PB = m:n by BPT.

wrong_options.1: n is the second part of the ratio. Drawing through nth arc gives ratio n:m, not m:n.
wrong_options.2: m+n is the last arc, which is joined to B.
wrong_options.3: m-n would give wrong division.

medium.question: Two tangents are drawn from an external point P to a circle. If the distance from P to the center O is 13 cm and the radius is 5 cm, what is the length of each tangent?

wrong_options.1: 10 cm would need OP² - r² = 100, so OP² = 125, giving OP ≈ 11.18 cm.
wrong_options.2: 8 cm would need OP² - r² = 64, so OP² = 89, giving OP ≈ 9.43 cm.
wrong_options.3: 14 cm would need OP² - r² = 196, so OP² = 221, giving OP ≈ 14.87 cm.

medium.question: In the construction of a triangle similar to ΔABC with scale factor m/n (m < n), how many arcs are marked on the auxiliary ray and through which arc is the parallel drawn?

explanation.correct: For scale factor m/n, mark n equal arcs (denominator). Join nth arc to the base vertex. Draw parallel through the mth arc (numerator).

wrong_options.1: We mark n arcs (denominator), not m arcs (numerator).
wrong_options.2: Drawing through (m+n)th arc is incorrect — through mth arc only.
wrong_options.3: For similar triangle construction, arcs = denominator, not sum.

medium.question: What is the justification for drawing the circle on OP as diameter when constructing tangents from P?
options: The angle subtended by diameter is a right angle
The circle has the same area as the original
The diameter is perpendicular to the tangent

explanation.correct: We need ∠OTP = 90° (Tangent-Radius theorem). For any point T on the circle with diameter OP, ∠OTP = 90° (angle in a semicircle). So T is the point where the tangent touches the circle.

wrong_options.1: Area equivalence is not the reason.
wrong_options.2: Diameter is not necessarily perpendicular to the tangent — radius at point of contact is.
wrong_options.3: Chord equality is irrelevant here.

medium.question: While constructing a triangle similar to a given triangle with scale factor m/n where m > n, the new triangle will be formed by:
options: Extending the sides of the original triangle
Drawing the triangle inside the original
Keeping the base same and reducing the height

explanation.correct: When m > n (enlargement), we extend the sides of the original triangle so the new triangle encloses the old one.

wrong_options.1: Drawing inside would give scale factor < 1.
wrong_options.2: Keeping base same and reducing height gives a different triangle, not similar.
wrong_options.3: The construction uses the same base vertex and extends the sides.

medium.question: From an external point P, tangents PT₁ and PT₂ are drawn. If the angle T₁PT₂ = 90°, then the locus of P for a fixed circle of radius r is:

explanation.correct: If ∠T₁PT₂ = 90°, then quadrilateral OT₁PT₂ has ∠T₁ = ∠T₂ = 90° and ∠T₁PT₂ = 90°, so ∠T₁OT₂ = 90°. OT₁ = OT₂ = r, so by Pythagoras, OP² = r² + r² = 2r², OP = r√2. So P lies on a circle of radius r√2.

wrong_options.1: OP = r means P is on the original circle itself, giving only 1 tangent.
wrong_options.2: A straight line would need a linear relationship.
wrong_options.3: Parabola is not formed by this geometric condition.

medium.question: A 10 cm line segment is to be divided in the ratio 2:3. What will be the lengths of the two parts?

explanation.correct: Total units = 2 + 3 = 5. First part = (2/5) × 10 = 4 cm. Second part = (3/5) × 10 = 6 cm.

wrong_options.1: 2 cm and 8 cm give ratio 1:4, not 2:3.
wrong_options.2: 3 cm and 7 cm give ratio 3:7, not 2:3.
wrong_options.3: 5 cm and 5 cm give ratio 1:1, not 2:3.

medium.question: In the construction of a tangent at a point on a circle, which tool is used to construct the perpendicular to the radius?

explanation.correct: We use a compass to construct a 90° angle (by constructing perpendicular bisector) and a ruler to draw the line. Both compass and ruler are required.

wrong_options.1: Only a ruler cannot construct a perpendicular without measurements.
wrong_options.2: Only a compass can mark arcs but cannot draw the line.
wrong_options.3: Protractor is not used in geometric constructions (only ruler and compass).

medium.question: Two tangents drawn from a point P to a circle of radius 6 cm are each of length 8 cm. Find OP.

explanation.correct: By Tangent-Radius theorem and Pythagoras: OP² = PT² + r² = 8² + 6² = 64 + 36 = 100. OP = 10 cm.

wrong_options.1: 12 cm would need PT² + r² = 144, so PT² = 144 - 36 = 108, PT = √108 ≈ 10.39 cm.
wrong_options.2: 14 cm would give PT² = 196 - 36 = 160, PT = √160 ≈ 12.65 cm.
wrong_options.3: 2√7 ≈ 5.29 cm is too small to be OP (must be > r = 6 cm).

medium.question: If in the construction of a similar triangle, the scale factor is given as 0.4, what fraction should we use?

explanation.correct: 0.4 = 4/10 = 2/5 in simplest form. Scale factor = 2/5 means mark 5 arcs and draw parallel through 2nd arc.

wrong_options.1: 4/10 is equivalent but not in simplest form. Simplest is 2/5.

complex.question: A circle of radius 5 cm has two tangents from an external point P inclined at 60°. Find the distance OP.

explanation.correct:
If angle between tangents = 60°, then sin(60°/2) = sin(30°) = r/OP → 1/2 = 5/OP → OP = 10 cm. Wait, that gives 10 cm. Let me recheck.

Actually, sin(θ/2) = r/OP where θ = angle between tangents.
sin(30°) = 5/OP → 1/2 = 5/OP → OP = 10 cm.

So answer should be 10 cm, but let me check the options again. Option 0 is 10 cm, option 2 is 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 cm.

Let me verify: In the quadrilateral, ∠APB = 60°, ∠A = ∠B = 90°, so ∠AOB = 120°.
In ΔOAP, sin(60°) = OA/OP → √3/2 = 5/OP → OP = 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 cm.

Actually, I need to be careful. sin(θ/2) where θ is angle between tangents:
sin(30°) = r/OP → 1/2 = 5/OP → OP = 10 cm? But that contradicts the quadrilateral method.

Let me re-derive. ∠APB = 60°, OA = r = 5 cm, OA ⟂ AP.
In right ΔOAP, ∠APO = 30° (since the line OP bisects ∠APB = 60°).
sin(30°) = OA/OP = 5/OP → 1/2 = 5/OP → OP = 10 cm.

But wait, OA is the radius and AP is the tangent. OA is NOT the hypotenuse.
In right ΔOAP, right angle at A (OA ⟂ AP).
∠APO = 30° (half of ∠APB).
So sin(30°) = opposite/hypotenuse = OA/OP = 5/OP.
1/2 = 5/OP → OP = 10 cm.

Hmm, but let me verify with another method:
In ΔOAP, we have OA = 5, ∠OAP = 90°, ∠APO = 30°.
So tan(30°) = OA/AP → 1/√3 = 5/AP → AP = 5√3.
OP² = OA² + AP² = 25 + 75 = 100 → OP = 10 cm. ✓

So OP = 10 cm is correct.

wrong_options.2: 10/√3 ≈ 5.77 cm. This would mean OP ≈ 5.77, but then sin⁻¹(5/5.77) ≈ 60°, which is ∠APO, not 30°.
wrong_options.3: 5 cm = r. If OP = r, P is on the circle, only 1 tangent exists.

complex.question: A 14 cm long line segment is to be divided in the ratio 3:4. A ray is drawn and 7 equal arcs are marked. If the distance from A to A₇ (last arc) is 7 cm, what is the length saved per arc?

explanation.correct: If 7 equal arcs cover 7 cm, each arc length = 7/7 = 1 cm. The arcs can be of any convenient length on the auxiliary ray. Their length does not affect the division ratio because BPT uses equal divisions regardless of the actual arc length.

wrong_options.1: 0.5 cm would require 14 arcs for 7 cm distance.
wrong_options.2: 2 cm per arc would require only 3.5 arcs for 7 cm.
wrong_options.3: 7 cm per arc means only 1 arc, but we need 7 arcs.

complex.question: From an external point P, tangents PT₁ and PT₂ are drawn. If OT₁ = 4 cm and PT₁ = 3 cm, find the area of quadrilateral OT₁PT₂.

explanation.correct:
OT₁ = OT₂ = r = 4 cm. PT₁ = PT₂ = 3 cm. Both triangles OT₁P and OT₂P are right-angled at T₁ and T₂.
Area of each = (1/2) × 4 × 3 = 6 cm².
Total area of quadrilateral = 6 + 6 = 12 cm².
Alternatively, quadrilateral OT₁PT₂ is a kite with diagonals OP and T₁T₂.
OP = √(4² + 3²) = 5 cm.

wrong_options.0: 24 cm² would be the area of a rectangle 4 × 6, not the kite.
wrong_options.2: 48 cm² is too large for these dimensions.
wrong_options.3: 6 cm² is only the area of one triangle, not both.

complex.question: Construct ΔABC with AB = 4 cm, BC = 5 cm, CA = 6 cm. Then the scale factor to construct ΔA'BC' ∼ ΔABC with A'C' = 9 cm is:

explanation.correct: Original AC = 6 cm. New A'C' = 9 cm. Scale factor = new/original = 9/6 = 3/2 = 1.5.

wrong_options.1: 4/3 would give A'C' = (4/3) × 6 = 8 cm, not 9 cm.
wrong_options.2: 9/5 would use BC as reference, but A'C' corresponds to AC.
wrong_options.3: 9/4 would use AB as reference, but A'C' corresponds to AC.

complex.question: In the construction of tangents from P to a circle, if the circle drawn on OP as diameter intersects the original circle at T₁ and T₂, what is ∠OT₁P?

explanation.correct: Since OP is the diameter of the new circle and T₁ lies on this circle, ∠OT₁P is the angle in a semicircle, which is always 90°. This matches the requirement that the tangent is perpendicular to the radius OT₁.

wrong_options.1: 60° would not guarantee the tangent condition (90°).
wrong_options.2: 45° would not be sufficient for tangent.
wrong_options.3: 30° is an acute angle, not enough for tangency.

complex.question: Two circles of radii 5 cm and 3 cm have their centers 9 cm apart. How many common tangents can be drawn to them?

explanation.correct:
Distance between centers = d = 9 cm. Sum of radii = 5 + 3 = 8 cm. Since d > sum of radii (9 > 8), the circles do not intersect and are externally separate. For externally separate circles, 4 common tangents exist (2 direct + 2 transverse).

- If d = |r₁ - r₂|: 1 common tangent (touch internally)
- If d < |r₁ - r₂|: 0 common tangents (one inside other)

Actually, in NCERT Class 10 Constructions, we only construct tangents from external point to a SINGLE circle, not common tangents between two circles. The question is about common tangents between two circles.

wrong_options.1: 1 tangent exists when circles touch internally (d = |r₁-r₂|).
wrong_options.2: 3 tangents exist when circles touch externally (d = r₁+r₂).

complex.question: If we construct a triangle similar to ΔABC with scale factor 5/2 by extending sides, how many extra arcs beyond the denominator need to be marked?

explanation.correct: Scale factor = 5/2. Denominator = 2, numerator = 5. We mark 2 arcs (denominator) on the auxiliary ray. Since numerator > denominator, we need to extend: from the 2nd arc (the last), we go 3 more steps to reach the 5th arc. So 3 extra arcs beyond the denominator.

wrong_options.1: 2 extra would reach the 4th arc, not the 5th.
wrong_options.2: 5 is the numerator, not the number of extra arcs.
wrong_options.3: 7 is the sum of numerator and denominator.

complex.question: A point P is at distance d from the center of a circle of radius r. For what value of d/r will the angle between the tangents be 120°?

explanation.correct: If angle between tangents = 120°, then sin(60°) = r/d → √3/2 = r/d → d = 2r/√3 → d/r = 2/√3.

wrong_options.1: √3/2 would give d = 2r/√3 inverted.
wrong_options.2: d/r = 2 gives angle = 60° (since sin(30°) = r/2r = 1/2).
wrong_options.3: d/r = 1/2 gives d < r, point inside circle, no tangents.

complex.question: In ΔABC, AB = 5 cm, BC = 6 cm, ∠B = 90°. A similar triangle A'BC' is constructed with scale factor 4/3. What is the area of A'BC'?

explanation.correct:
Area scales as (scale factor)². Original area = (1/2) × 5 × 6 = 15 cm². New area = (4/3)² × 15 = (16/9) × 15 = 80/3 ≈ 26.67 cm².

Option A: (4/3)² × 15 = (16/9) × 15 = 80/3 ← correct.
Option C: (1/2) × (4/3 × 5) × (4/3 × 6) = (1/2) × (20/3) × 8 = (1/2) × 160/3 = 80/3 ← also correct.
Both A and C give the same result.

wrong_options.0: A is correct but C is also correct.
wrong_options.1: 4/3 × 15 = 20 is wrong (area scales by k², not k).
wrong_options.2: C is correct but A is also correct.

complex.question: From an external point, the length of tangent to a circle is 12 cm and the distance from the center is 15 cm. Find the radius and the angle between the tangents.

wrong_options.1: r = 8 cm would give r² = 64, but OP² - PT² = 81, so r = 9 cm.
wrong_options.2: r = 10 cm would give OP² - PT² = 100, but 225 - 144 = 81.
wrong_options.3: θ = 60° would need sin(30°) = r/OP = 9/15 = 0.6, but sin(30°) = 0.5, so this is incorrect.

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Geometric Construction Shortcuts Using Vedic Proportions (Samashti — समष्टि)
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: Vedic mathematics offers quick proportional reasoning that helps verify construction measurements without tedious calculations.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: When dividing a line segment, quickly verify part lengths using fraction-to-decimal conversion.

examples.problem: Quickly find the lengths when a 13.2 cm line is divided in ratio 4:7.
examples.explanation: Total parts = 11. Each part = 13.2/11 = 1.2 cm. Using Vedic method: 13.2 × 4/11 = 13.2 ÷ 11 × 4 = 1.2 × 4 = 4.8 cm.
steps: Step 1: Write 13.2 × 4 = 52.8
Step 2: Divide by 11: 52.8 ÷ 11 = 4.8 (using the Vedic rule for division by 11)
Step 3: First part = 4.8 cm, second part = 13.2 - 4.8 = 8.4 cm

vedic_math_shortcuts.title: Ekadhikena Purvena (एकाधिकेन पूर्वेण) — 'One more than the previous'
vedic_math_shortcuts.concept: For squaring numbers ending in 5, and for quickly computing tangent lengths that involve perfect squares.
vedic_math_shortcuts.real_numbers_application: Quick computation of PT² = OP² - r² when OP and r are given.

examples.problem: Find the length of tangent when OP = 13 cm and r = 5 cm.
steps: Step 2: PT = √144 = 12 cm (using Vedic square root estimation)
Tip: Memorize common Pythagorean triples: (5,12,13), (3,4,5), (8,15,17), (7,24,25)
examples.usage: Tangent length always uses Pythagoras: PT² = OP² - r². Recognize the triple (5,12,13) for instant answer.

flowcharts.title: Decision Flowchart: Which Construction Method to Use?

steps.action: What do you need to construct?
Is it dividing a line segment in a ratio?
Draw ray → mark (m+n) arcs → draw parallel through mth arc
Is it constructing a similar triangle?
Scale factor = m/n. Is m > n?
Mark n arcs on ray → draw parallel through mth arc → get new triangle
Is it constructing tangents to a circle?
Is the point ON the circle or OUTSIDE?
ON circle: draw ⟂ to radius. OUTSIDE: draw circle with diameter OP, join P to intersections
Draw circle with center O and given radius r
Find midpoint M of OP (perpendicular bisector)
Draw circle with center M, radius MO = MP
Mark intersections T₁, T₂ of both circles
Join PT₁ and PT₂ — these are the required tangents

common_misconceptions: Any point on a circle can have multiple tangents — FALSE: Exactly ONE tangent exists at a given point on a circle, and it is perpendicular to the radius at that point.
A tangent touches the circle at exactly one point and can cross the circle elsewhere — FALSE: A tangent touches at exactly one point and does NOT intersect the circle anywhere else.

While constructing a similar triangle with scale factor m/n, we should mark n arcs on the ray only when m < n — FALSE: We ALWAYS mark n arcs (the denominator), regardless of whether m < n or m > n. When m > n, we extend the ray further.
The arcs marked on the auxiliary ray must be exactly 1 cm each — FALSE: The arcs can be of any convenient length; they just need to be EQUAL. The ratio depends on the count, not the arc length.
When dividing a line segment in ratio m:n, we draw the parallel through the mth arc which gives AP:PB = m:n — CORRECT: This is by BPT, as AAₘ:AₘAₘ₊ₙ = m:n = AP:PB.

The construction for dividing a line segment and constructing a similar triangle use the same BPT principle — CORRECT: Both use Thales theorem, but the arc marking differs: (m+n) arcs for division, n arcs for similar triangle.
From an external point at distance 2r from center, the angle between tangents is 90° — FALSE: When OP = 2r, sin(θ/2) = r/2r = 1/2, so θ/2 = 30°, θ = 60°. For 90°, we need sin(45°) = r/OP → OP = r√2.

Tangent construction from an external point works only if the point is outside the circle — TRUE: If P is on the circle, different construction (perpendicular at P). If P is inside, no tangent exists.
